strengths: The paper targets an important and relatively under-served problem: foundation models for time-series classification rather than forecasting. A lightweight frozen encoder pretrained only on synthetic data is a useful direction if validated robustly.

The empirical scope is broad: UCR, UEA, HAR, and EEG benchmarks are considered, with comparisons to tabular, forecasting, vision-adapted, and time-series classification foundation models. The reported averages for Mantis are consistently strong, e.g. 0.8195 on UCR vs 0.8029 for the strongest listed non-Mantis baseline, 0.7420 on UEA-27 vs 0.7199 for NuTime, and leading averages on HAR and EEG.

The ablations are unusually detailed. The manuscript separately studies synthetic pretraining data, tokenizer branches, transformer variants, intermediate-layer selection, token aggregation, self-ensembling, contrastive losses, augmentations, adapters, and predictors. These analyses make several useful observations, especially that intermediate representations can outperform final layers for frozen time-series feature extraction.

The model is practically appealing: the architecture is small, and the complexity analysis reports competitive accuracy with only a few million effective parameters and low inference cost relative to large vision and forecasting foundation models.
The synthetic-only pretraining setup is a meaningful attempt to avoid leakage from common time-series archives and is a plausible contribution beyond simply scaling another real-data corpus.
weaknesses: The main evaluation protocol appears to tune important choices directly on the reported benchmark tasks. The paper selects the best intermediate layer, aggregation, predictor normalization, self-ensembling settings, and in some cases fusion based on UCR performance, then reports UCR as a central result. Without a held-out meta-validation set or nested model-selection protocol, the state-of-the-art claims are likely optimistic and hard to interpret.

The term zero-shot is potentially misleading. The downstream setting uses all training labels to fit logistic regression or random forests, sometimes with benchmark-level choices of classifier and scaling. This is frozen-encoder transfer or linear probing, not label-free zero-shot classification; the manuscript partly clarifies this, but the framing still overstates the zero-shot nature.

Reproducibility is insufficient for a paper whose claims rely on many implementation details. The abstract says source code is available, but the link is blank. I also could not find key pretraining details such as optimizer, learning rate, batch size, training schedule, projector architecture, hardware, and exact random-seed protocol for the main Mantis pretraining runs.

The strongest claims conflate several distinct contributions. The best UCR numbers involve self-ensembling and cross-model embedding fusion with large external models, while the core Mantis-only gains are more modest. The paper should more clearly separate the value of the pretrained Mantis encoder from the value of benchmark-tuned test-time feature engineering and fusion.

Comparisons to specialized supervised time-series classifiers are limited. The manuscript includes some older or extracted baselines on UCR-91, but does not adequately compare against recent strong TSC methods such as ROCKET-family/Hydra/MultiRocket-style approaches across the main full benchmarks. Thus the claim of matching strong specialized approaches is not fully supported.

Several benchmark modifications reduce comparability: UEA excludes three datasets and subsamples InsectWingbeat, HAR/EEG collections are assembled with custom splits, and some baselines time out or are marked NaN. These choices may be reasonable, but the paper needs clearer justification and sensitivity analysis.

The multivariate handling is simplistic in the main experiments: channels are encoded independently and concatenated, causing feature dimension to grow with channel count and delaying cross-channel interaction until the classifier. The adapter experiment is promising but only preliminary and not integrated into the main method.

The limitations and ethics discussion is very thin. The impact statement says no societal consequences need highlighting despite experiments on EEG, healthcare-adjacent, and human activity data. Limitations around privacy, clinical misuse, domain shift, calibration, and failure modes deserve more careful treatment.

strengths: The paper targets an important and under-served problem: foundation models for time-series classification rather than forecasting, and the lightweight focus is practically relevant.

Mantis has a simple, plausible design: fixed-token convolutional/statistical tokenization, contrastive pretraining, and frozen-encoder downstream use. The tokenizer branches and intermediate-layer observations are reasonable and potentially useful.
The empirical scope is broad, covering UCR, UEA, HAR, and EEG collections, with many competitive baselines from tabular, forecasting, vision-adapted, and time-series-specific foundation models.

The appendix contains useful ablations on pretraining data, tokenizer components, transformer variants, pretraining objective, augmentation, output-token aggregation, self-ensembling, adapters, and layer choice.
The model is small and appears computationally attractive relative to many foundation-model baselines.
weaknesses: The central claim of establishing a new state of the art is not fully supported. The reported gains over strong baselines are often modest, sometimes depend on self-ensembling or cross-model feature fusion, and are not accompanied by statistical tests over datasets or a careful uncertainty analysis for the headline averages.

The evaluation protocol raises serious concerns. The paper repeatedly selects the best intermediate layer based on benchmark performance, apparently using the same benchmark being reported. This effectively tunes on the test benchmark and makes the reported zero-shot/frozen-encoder numbers optimistic unless a separate validation/meta-validation protocol is used.

The term zero-shot feature extraction is misleading: all downstream evaluations train a supervised classifier using task labels. That is a frozen-encoder or linear-probing setting, not zero-shot classification in the usual sense.

Several comparisons are hard to interpret. The paper changes probes between sections, replacing logistic regression with random forests for computational reasons and only asserts that rankings are unaffected. Some baselines are modified from their original intended use, while Mantis benefits from extensive test-time choices tailored to the benchmark.

Dataset handling weakens comparability: UEA excludes several datasets and subsamples InsectWingbeat; large HAR/EEG collections include custom splits and time limits; tabular baselines produce NaNs on some datasets. These choices may be reasonable, but they make broad average comparisons less decisive.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The abstract says source code is available but the link is blank, and important details such as CauKer generation settings, training compute, exact seeds, model-selection protocol, and full hyperparameter search are not sufficiently specified for reliable independent reproduction.

The paper lacks a serious limitations and ethics discussion. The impact statement says no societal consequences need highlighting despite applications to healthcare, EEG, human activity recognition, and potentially sensitive physiological data.

Presentation is generally understandable but somewhat overclaims. Some tables are dense, there are minor typos/formatting issues, and the narrative sometimes treats useful engineering improvements as stronger scientific conclusions than the evidence warrants.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and relatively under-served setting: foundation models for time-series classification rather than forecasting. The proposed model is lightweight, practically motivated, and clearly targeted at frozen-encoder feature extraction.

The empirical evaluation is broad and convincing overall: UCR-91, full UCR-128, UEA-27, HAR, and EEG benchmarks are compared against self-supervised time-series methods, statistical features, tabular FMs, forecasting FMs, vision-adapted FMs, and a prior classification TSFM. Mantis is consistently competitive or best, with especially strong results given its small parameter count.

The ablations are unusually thorough. The paper separately studies synthetic pre-training data, tokenizer branches, transformer variants, intermediate-layer representations, output-token aggregation, self-ensembling, contrastive loss choice, augmentations, and predictor normalization. These analyses support the main design choices rather than only reporting headline benchmark numbers.

The intermediate-layer finding is a useful conceptual contribution beyond this specific architecture. Showing that intermediate layers improve frozen feature extraction across Mantis and other TSFMs is practically valuable, and the pruning/runtime analysis makes the contribution more deployable.
The use of purely synthetic pre-training data is significant for avoiding train/test overlap with common archives and for reducing dependence on large curated real-world corpora.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol appears to use benchmark test performance to choose intermediate layers and test-time feature extraction variants. If layer choice, aggregation, interpolation/self-ensemble settings, or fusion choices are selected using the same test suites on which final accuracy is reported, the results are likely optimistic. A validation-only or held-out benchmark selection protocol would make the central performance claims stronger.

Reproducibility is not yet adequate for a top-tier submission. The abstract says source code is available but the link is blank in the manuscript, and key pre-training details such as optimizer, batch size, number of epochs/updates for the final model, CauKer generation configuration, compute budget, and random seed handling are not fully specified in the main experimental setup.

The term “zero-shot feature extraction” is potentially misleading, since downstream labels are used to train logistic regression or random forests. The paper clarifies this, but the headline claims should consistently say frozen-encoder probing or frozen feature extraction to avoid overstating the setting.

Some comparisons are not perfectly controlled. The paper switches from logistic regression to random forests for the broader breakdown, uses improved/pruned intermediate layers for many baselines, excludes or subsamples some UEA datasets, and reports NaNs for tabular FMs under time/memory limits. These choices are mostly reasonable, but they complicate interpretation of exact ranking claims.

The method combines several components from recent practice: convolutional tokenization, synthetic contrastive pre-training, intermediate-layer probing, self-ensembling, and embedding fusion. The overall system is effective, but the architectural originality is moderate; much of the novelty is in careful integration and empirical understanding.

The limitations and ethics discussion is thin. The paper notes future directions, but does not seriously discuss failure modes in healthcare/EEG/HAR deployments, calibration, domain shift, dataset licensing constraints, or risks from using benchmark-tuned model selection.
